Q: Create extension that exposes MCP endpoints that CoPilot can see A:

The problem isn't your extension or your endpoints. The problem is how Copilot discovers MCP tools.

Exposing commands in VS Code is not the same as exposing tools to Copilot.

They are different systems:

VS Code commands → manual actions (Command Palette)

MCP tools → tools that the model can discover and execute automatically

Copilot doesn't inspect your extension or your commands. It can only use tools that come from MCP servers explicitly registered on the host (VS Code).

What's happening?

Currently:

Your extension is running

Your MCP server is running

The endpoints are working ❌ Copilot doesn't see them

This means your server is isolated.

Copilot only sees the tools when:

VS Code (MCP host)

→ launches/connects your server

→ MCP handshake

→ tools/list

→ registers tools

→ Copilot can invoke them

If the server is run manually in a terminal, there is never a connection with Copilot.

The missing step

You must register your MCP server in VS Code, not just run it.

Create:

.vscode/mcp.json

or user config:

mcp.json

Minimal example:

{

"servers": {

"hello-world": {

"type": "stdio",

"command": "node",

"args": ["./dist/server.js"]

}

}

}

This allows:

VS Code to start the server

VS Code to initialize

VS Code to call tools/list

Copilot to receive the tools

Without this → Copilot never discovers them.

Why DB Client works

Extensions like Database Client/MySQL:

automatically register their MCP server

the host starts them

tools/list is executed

Copilot displays them

Your extension only exposes commands; it doesn't register as an MCP provider.

Verification Checklist

Before testing:

Server declared in mcp.json

Stdio or SSE transport is working correctly

Copilot in Agent Mode

`tools/list` responds

Logs show `initialize` + `tools/list`

If you don't see `tools/list` in the logs → the host is not connected.

Q: Does malloc failure imply ENOMEM? A:

I checked the man page for malloc ...

You checked a man page for malloc. One particular implementation.

But in general malloc() is free to set errno to any value no matter what it returns.

The (draft) C11 standard documentation for malloc() does not document any setting of errno by malloc().

Furthermore, per C11, 7.5 Errors <errno.h>, paragraph 3 (bolding mine):

... The value of errno may be set to nonzero by a library function call whether or not there is an error, provided the use of errno is not documented in the description of the function in this International Standard.

C17 and C23 are similar.

In general, you can't even rely on errno remaining zero after any malloc() call.

and also, ChatGPT says so too...

And now you know what to think of ChatGPT.
